When is a random process wide-sense stationary?
column2: When its mean is constant and its autocorrelation E[X(t+τ)X(t)] depends only on the lag τ.

column1: State the Wiener–Khinchin theorem.
column2: The PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation, S_X(f) = ∫R_X(τ)e^(−j2πfτ)dτ; the power is R_X(0) = ∫S_X df. A valid R_X must have a nonnegative transform.

column1: Autocorrelation and PSD of A cos(2πf₀t + Θ) with Θ uniform?
column2: R_X(τ) = (A²/2)cos(2πf₀τ); two spectral lines of weight A²/4 at ±f₀; power A²/2.

column1: How does an LTI filter change a WSS process's PSD?
column2: S_Y(f) = |H(f)|²S_X(f); the mean becomes H(0)m_X. Phase does not matter for the PSD.

column1: Equivalent noise bandwidth of a one-pole RC low-pass?
column2: B_N = (π/2)f_3dB. White noise of two-sided PSD N₀/2 gives output power N₀B_N, with autocorrelation ∝ e^(−|τ|/RC).

column1: Why is the noise on a capacitor √(kT/C) whatever the resistor?
column2: A larger R gives more noise density but proportionally less bandwidth; the integral of 4kTR|H|² over frequency is kT/C. 1 pF gives 64 µV rms at 300 K.

column1: PSD of random polar NRZ data of amplitude A and bit time T?
column2: A²T sinc²(fT): nulls at multiples of 1/T; 90.3% of the power lies below 1/T.

column1: What happens if wideband noise is sampled without an anti-alias filter?
column2: All the noise folds into [0, f_s/2], so the in-band density rises by about 2B_N/f_s.

column1: What is kT₀ in dBm/Hz, and the noise in 1 MHz and 20 MHz?
column2: −174 dBm/Hz (4.00 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz at 290 K); −114 dBm in 1 MHz, −101 dBm in 20 MHz.

column1: Relate noise factor and noise temperature.
column2: F = 1 + T_e/T₀, with T₀ = 290 K. NF 1 dB ≈ 75 K; NF 3 dB ≈ 289 K.

column1: Noise figure of a passive loss at room temperature?
column2: Equal to its loss: 2 dB of cable before the LNA adds 2 dB to the receiver's noise figure.

column1: State the Friis cascade formula and its lesson.
column2: F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ + (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂) + …: the first stage's noise figure dominates if its gain is high, so put a low-noise amplifier first.

column1: Receiver sensitivity in decibels?
column2: P_sens = −174 + 10log₁₀B + NF + SNR_req (+ implementation margin) dBm.

column1: Convert between SNR and Eb/N0.
column2: SNR = (E_b/N₀)(R_b/B); in dB, E_b/N₀ = SNR − 10log₁₀(R_b/B). C/N₀ = SNR·B.

column1: How does GPS work with signals below the noise floor?
column2: Correlating against the known code over long integration gives a processing gain: the C/N₀ (about 47 dB-Hz) matters, not the SNR in the 2 MHz bandwidth.

column1: Carson's rule?
column2: B_T = 2(Δf + W): about 99% of an FM signal's power for β ≳ 1. Broadcast FM: 2(75 + 15) = 180 kHz.

column1: Spectrum of tone FM?
column2: Lines at f_c ± nf_m with amplitudes J_n(β); the carrier vanishes at β = 2.405 and 5.520, which is used to calibrate deviation.

column1: Power efficiency of AM, and its value for a 100% tone?
column2: η = k_a²P_m/(1 + k_a²P_m); 1/3 for a full tone, so AM's output SNR is 4.77 dB below DSB's for the same received power.

column1: FM's output SNR for a tone above threshold?
column2: (3/2)β²γ with γ = S_R/(N₀W): the SNR grows with the square of the bandwidth expansion. β = 5 gives 15.7 dB over DSB.

column1: What is the FM threshold?
column2: Below a carrier-to-noise ratio of about 10 dB in the IF bandwidth, noise captures the phase (clicks) and the SNR collapses; FM's advantage ends there.

column1: Why does FM use pre-emphasis?
column2: Discriminator noise has a parabolic PSD (∝ f²), so boosting high audio frequencies before transmission and cutting them after reduces the noise: about 13 dB with 75 µs at 15 kHz.

column1: Which analog schemes match the baseband SNR γ?
column2: DSB-SC and SSB with coherent detection, and SSB in half the bandwidth.

column1: Nyquist's criterion for zero ISI?
column2: The folded spectrum Σ_k P(f − k/T) must be constant: the minimum bandwidth is 1/(2T), the ideal sinc pulse.

column1: Bandwidth of raised-cosine pulses with roll-off α?
column2: (1 + α)/(2T) at baseband, (1 + α)/T around a carrier. Splitting it as root-raised-cosine at each end makes the receive filter matched.

column1: PAM4's penalty against NRZ?
column2: At equal peak amplitude each of its three eyes is a third as tall: 9.54 dB of SNR (6.99 dB at equal average power). It halves the symbol rate.

column1: When does PAM4 beat NRZ?
column2: When the extra channel loss at NRZ's doubled Nyquist frequency exceeds 9.54 dB: steep (dielectric) loss favours PAM4; gentle loss, like a one-pole channel's 6 dB per octave, favours NRZ.

column1: Pulse response of a one-pole channel sampled at the end of each bit?
column2: Main cursor 1 − r, postcursors (1 − r)r^k with r = e^(−T/τ); worst-case NRZ eye 1 − 2r.

column1: What does a zero-forcing equalizer do, and what does it cost?
column2: It inverts the channel's pulse response over its taps to force the ISI to zero, but amplifies noise where the channel is weak.

column1: Overhead of 8b/10b, 64b/66b and 128b/130b coding?
What is the matched filter and its output SNR?
column2: h(t) = k s(T − t), the time-reversed pulse; its peak output SNR is 2E/N₀ for any pulse shape (Cauchy–Schwarz).

column1: Error probability between two signals at distance d?
column2: Q(d/√(2N₀)), with noise variance N₀/2 per dimension.

column1: BER of antipodal and of orthogonal binary signalling?
column2: Antipodal: Q(√(2E_b/N₀)), 9.59 dB for 10⁻⁵. Orthogonal (and on-off at equal average energy): Q(√(E_b/N₀)), 3 dB worse.

column1: How much does the best one-pole filter lose against the matched filter on a rectangular pulse?
column2: 0.89 dB (81.45% of the SNR), with f_3dB ≈ 0.2/T.

column1: MAP threshold for ±√E with unequal priors?
column2: t = (N₀/(4√E)) ln(P₋/P₊): it moves toward the less likely symbol.

column1: What is the union bound?
column2: P_e ≤ Σ_{j≠i} Q(d_ij/√(2N₀)); at high SNR the nearest neighbours dominate.

column1: Values of Q⁻¹ to remember?
Why does QPSK have the same BER as BPSK?
column2: With Gray coding each bit rides on its own orthogonal dimension (I or Q) as independent BPSK with energy E_b: twice the rate in the same bandwidth at the same E_b/N₀.

column1: Symbol-error approximation for M-PSK?
column2: P_s ≈ 2Q(√(2E_s/N₀) sin(π/M)); 8-PSK costs 3.57 dB per bit against QPSK.

column1: Symbol-error probability of square M-QAM?
column2: p = 2(1 − 1/√M)Q(√(3E_s/((M − 1)N₀))) per dimension and P_s = 1 − (1 − p)²; Gray BER ≈ P_s/log₂M.

column1: Why is 16-QAM better than 16-PSK?
column2: It uses the plane more efficiently: larger minimum distance for the same average energy, 4.20 dB asymptotically.

column1: Noncoherent and differential alternatives?
column2: DPSK ½e^(−E_b/N₀) (0.75 dB worse than BPSK at 10⁻⁵); noncoherent BFSK ½e^(−E_b/2N₀) (3.76 dB worse). They need no carrier phase.

column1: How does EVM relate to SNR?
column2: SNR_EVM = 1/EVM² if the impairments are noise-like: 3.5% ↔ 29.1 dB, 8% ↔ 21.9 dB. Independent impairments add as 1/SNR_total = Σ1/SNR_i.

column1: Spectral efficiency of M-ary modulation with raised-cosine pulses?
column2: η = log₂M/(1 + α) b/s/Hz.

column1: Entropy of a source, and what it limits?
column2: H = −Σp log₂p bits per symbol, at most log₂M: the minimum average length of any lossless code.

column1: How does Huffman coding work, and how close is it to entropy?
column2: Repeatedly merge the two least likely symbols; H ≤ L̄ < H + 1, with equality when every probability is a power of 1/2.

column1: Capacity of the binary symmetric and erasure channels?
State the Shannon–Hartley theorem.
column2: C = B log₂(1 + S/N) for an AWGN channel; 20 MHz at 20 dB gives 133 Mb/s.

column1: What is the Shannon limit on Eb/N0?
column2: E_b/N₀ ≥ (2^η − 1)/η: 0 dB at 1 b/s/Hz, 1.76 dB at 2, 5.74 dB at 4, and ln 2 = −1.59 dB as η → 0.

column1: Power-limited versus bandwidth-limited regimes?
column2: At low SNR capacity is linear in power (C → 1.443 S/N₀); at high SNR each extra b/s/Hz costs about 3 dB.

column1: What is water-filling?
column2: For parallel channels, pour power P_i = (μ − N_i/g_i)⁺ until the budget is spent: strong channels get more, very weak ones none.

column1: Value of soft decisions at rate 1/2?
column2: About 1.6 dB of E_b/N₀ for BPSK, from comparing the soft and hard-decision capacities.

column1: How many errors can a code with minimum distance d correct and detect?
column2: Correct t = ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋, detect d − 1, fill d − 1 erasures.

column1: The (7,4) Hamming code in one line?
column2: Rate 4/7, d_min = 3, corrects one error per block; a perfect code. Coding gain 2.34 dB soft, only 0.58 dB hard.

column1: What does a CRC of degree r guarantee?
column2: It detects every burst of r bits or fewer, and misses about 2⁻ʳ of random error patterns. NR uses CRC24A/B/C, 16, 11 and 6.

column1: Asymptotic coding gain, soft and hard?
column2: Soft 10log₁₀(R·d_min); hard about 10log₁₀(R(t + 1)), roughly 3 dB less.

column1: Reed–Solomon codes in one line?
column2: RS(n, k) over GF(2^m) corrects t = (n − k)/2 symbol errors, so long bit bursts: KP4 RS(544,514) has t = 15 and 5.84% overhead.

column1: How does the Viterbi algorithm decode a convolutional code?
column2: Add–compare–select: for every trellis state keep the lowest-metric path into it; 2^(K−1) states. The K = 7 (171,133) code has d_free = 10.

column1: What are LDPC and polar codes used for in 5G NR?
column2: LDPC (base graphs BG1 and BG2) for data channels; polar codes for control and broadcast.

column1: How close do the best practical codes get to capacity?
column2: About 0.5–1 dB from the constrained limit at long block lengths.

column1: Free-space path loss formula?
column2: 32.45 + 20log₁₀f_MHz + 20log₁₀d_km dB: 6 dB per doubling of distance or frequency (with isotropic antennas).

column1: Two-ray model beyond the breakpoint?
column2: Beyond d_BP = 4h_t h_r/λ, P_r ≈ P_tG_tG_r h_t²h_r²/d⁴: 40 dB per decade, independent of frequency.

column1: How is shadowing handled in a link budget?
column2: As a lognormal X_σ: add a margin of zσ (1.28σ for 90% coverage at the edge).

column1: Coherence bandwidth and delay spread?
column2: Inversely related: B_c(50%) ≈ 0.276/τ_rms for an exponential delay profile; signals wider than B_c see frequency-selective fading.

column1: Doppler shift and coherence time?
column2: f_D = v f_c/c (389 Hz at 3.5 GHz, 120 km/h); T_c ≈ 0.242/f_D at 50% correlation.

column1: BER of BPSK in Rayleigh fading?
column2: ½(1 − √(γ̄/(1 + γ̄))) ≈ 1/(4γ̄): 44 dB for 10⁻⁵ instead of 9.6 dB in AWGN.

column1: What does diversity of order L do?
column2: Error rates fall as γ̄⁻ᴸ: L-branch MRC gives ≈ C(2L−1, L)(4γ̄)⁻ᴸ. Two branches gain a factor of about 135 at 20 dB.

column1: Rayleigh outage for a fade margin M?
column2: About 1/M (linear): one decade per 10 dB of margin.

column1: Why are OFDM subcarriers spaced by 1/T?
column2: Over an interval T each sinc spectrum is zero at the frequencies of all the other subcarriers, so they are orthogonal; the IFFT/FFT generates and separates them.

column1: What does the cyclic prefix do?
column2: If it is at least as long as the channel's memory, it turns linear convolution into circular, so each subcarrier sees one complex gain: Y[k] = H[k]X[k].

column1: NR numerology and cyclic prefix?
column2: Δf = 15·2^μ kHz; normal CP 144/2048 of the useful symbol (6.57% of the total): 4.69 µs at 15 kHz, 2.34 µs at 30 kHz.

column1: ICI from a carrier frequency offset ε (in spacings)?
column2: About (πε)²/3: −34.8 dB at 1%, −14.8 dB at 10%. Doppler gives about (πf_D/Δf)²/6.

column1: How do you choose an OFDM numerology?
column2: CP longer than the delay spread, and subcarrier spacing much larger than the Doppler and phase noise: wide-area low bands use narrow spacing, mmWave wide spacing.

column1: Why does OFDM have a high PAPR, and what does it cost?
column2: A sum of many independent subcarriers is nearly Gaussian; PAPR at 10⁻³ is about ln(N/10⁻³), 10–12 dB, forcing PA back-off and lower efficiency.

column1: What is DFT-spread OFDM?
column2: OFDM with a DFT before subcarrier mapping, giving a single-carrier-like signal with several dB lower PAPR; an NR uplink option.

column1: SNR of maximal-ratio combining?
column2: ‖h‖²E_s/N₀: mean Nγ̄ (array gain N) and diversity order N.

column1: What does Alamouti coding achieve?
column2: Diversity 2 at rate 1 with two transmit antennas and no transmitter channel knowledge, 3 dB below 1×2 MRC because the power is split.

column1: Gain and beamwidth of an N-element half-wavelength array?
column2: Gain N; half-power beamwidth about 101.5°/N at broadside.

column1: MIMO capacity formula?
column2: C = log₂det(I + (ρ/N_t)HHᴴ) = Σ log₂(1 + ρσ_i²/N_t): one stream per nonzero singular value.

column1: Why does MIMO capacity scale with min(N_t, N_r)?
column2: At high SNR each eigenmode adds about log₂ρ; rich scattering makes H full rank, while line of sight makes it nearly rank 1.

column1: Zero-forcing versus MMSE MIMO receivers?
column2: ZF inverts H (diversity N_r − N_t + 1, noise enhancement); MMSE adds (N_t/ρ)I before inverting and is never worse, approaching ZF at high SNR.

column1: NR peak rate per 100 MHz FR1 carrier with 4 layers of 256-QAM?
column2: About 2.34 Gb/s by the TS 38.306 formula.

column1: ALOHA throughputs?
column2: Pure S = Ge^(−2G), at most 1/(2e) = 0.184 at G = 0.5; slotted S = Ge^(−G), at most 1/e = 0.368 at G = 1.

column1: Erlang B and trunking gain?
column2: B = (A^c/c!)/Σ_{k≤c}A^k/k!; large pools run at higher occupancy for the same blocking (20 Erl at 2% needs 28 channels).

column1: Cellular reuse geometry and SIR?
column2: N = i² + ij + j², D/R = √(3N), SIR ≈ (√(3N))ⁿ/6 with six first-tier interferers: N = 7, n = 4 gives 18.7 dB.

column1: CDMA processing gain?
column2: G_p = R_c/R_b: the chip rate over the bit rate; single-cell users ≈ 1 + G_p/(E_b/I₀).

column1: How does CSMA/CA behave with n saturated stations?
column2: A slot succeeds with probability nτ(1 − τ)^(n−1), maximized at τ = 1/n, approaching 1/e.

column1: Max-SNR versus proportional-fair scheduling?
column2: Max-SNR maximizes throughput but starves users at the cell edge; proportional fair serves each user near its own fading peaks, gaining multi-user diversity with fairness.

column1: HARQ throughput with independent attempts?
column2: 1 − p of one attempt per block, for any attempt limit; mean transmissions 1/(1 − p) if unlimited, Σ_{k<M}pᵏ with at most M; residual failure p^M after M attempts.

column1: Ethernet bytes on the wire per frame?
column2: 8 preamble/SFD + 14 header + payload (46–1500) + 4 FCS + 12 inter-frame gap; 84 bytes minimum, so 14.88 million frames/s at 10 Gb/s.

column1: Usable hosts in an IPv4 /p subnet?
How does a router choose among overlapping prefixes?
column2: Longest-prefix match: the most specific matching entry wins.

column1: Link-state versus distance-vector routing?
column2: Link state floods the topology and runs Dijkstra; distance vector iterates Bellman–Ford with neighbours and can count to infinity after a failure.

column1: TCP's window limit and the bandwidth-delay product?
column2: Throughput ≤ W/RTT; to fill rate R a window of R × RTT is needed. 65 535 bytes unscaled; RFC 7323 scaling allows a shift of up to 14.

column1: The Mathis formula?
column2: R ≈ (MSS/RTT)√(3/(2p)) for AIMD with one loss every 1/p packets (random loss raises the constant about 7%, delayed ACKs lower it by √2): halving the RTT doubles it, and 1 Gb/s over 50 ms needs p below about 10⁻⁷.

column1: RFC 6298 retransmission timeout?
column2: RTO = SRTT + 4·RTTVAR, at least 1 s, with gains 1/8 for SRTT and 1/4 for RTTVAR.

column1: Name the OSI layers and what each adds.
column2: Physical (bits on a medium), link (frames, MAC addresses; Ethernet, Wi-Fi), network (packets, IP addresses, routing), transport (segments, ports; TCP, UDP), session, presentation, application. TCP/IP merges the top three into one application layer.

column1: Name the security triad and a control for each.
column2: Confidentiality (encryption, access control), integrity (MACs, signatures, hashes), availability (redundancy, rate limiting, DoS protection).

column1: IDS versus IPS?
column2: An IDS monitors and alerts, by signatures of known attacks or anomalies against a baseline; an IPS sits inline and blocks. Because attacks are rare, false positives dominate the alerts (the base-rate effect).

column1: What are port scanning and penetration testing for?
column2: Scanning enumerates open ports and services to find the attack surface; a penetration test is an authorized simulated attack that tries to exploit weaknesses and reports how far an attacker gets.

column1: The four parts of per-hop delay?
column2: Processing, queueing, transmission L/R and propagation d/s. A 1500-byte packet takes 12 µs at 1 Gb/s; 1000 km of fibre adds 5 ms.

column1: What does TCP do after a retransmission timeout?
column2: Sets ssthresh to half the data in flight (at least 2 segments), cwnd to 1 segment, restarts slow start, and doubles the RTO for the next timeout; Karn's rule skips RTT samples from retransmitted segments.

column1: Mean delay in an M/M/1 queue?
column2: T = 1/(μ − λ): five service times at 80% load and twenty at 95%, growing without bound as load approaches 1.
